reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Typically follows a low-energy fall in an older, often osteoporotic patient; the leg is characteristically shortened and externally rotated with pain on any movement
Fractures are broadly divided into intracapsular (subcapital/transcervical) and extracapsular (intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric), a distinction that governs both blood supply risk and treatment
The femoral head's blood supply runs retrograde up the neck, so displaced intracapsular fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union

Displaced intracapsular fractures in older patients are usually managed with arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement), whereas undisplaced or young patients' fractures are fixed to preserve the head
Extracapsular fractures retain a good blood supply and are typically treated with internal fixation such as a dynamic hip screw or intramedullary device
Early surgery (generally within about a day or two) and rapid mobilisation reduce complications; prolonged bed rest causes pressure sores, chest infection, and venous thromboembolism
A minority present with subtle or occult fractures and a normal-appearing radiograph; persistent inability to weight-bear warrants MRI or CT
Outcome depends heavily on comorbidity and pre-injury mobility; orthogeriatric co-management and bone-health assessment for future fracture prevention are integral
reference.pathophysiology: Hip fractures usually result from a fall onto the greater trochanter in bone weakened by osteoporosis, though high-energy trauma or pathological lesions can cause them at any age. The proximal femur is supplied largely by the medial femoral circumflex artery via retinacular vessels ascending the femoral neck beneath the capsule. Intracapsular fractures may tear these vessels, threatening viability of the femoral head and predisposing to avascular necrosis and non-union, especially when displaced. Extracapsular fractures occur through well-vascularised cancellous bone and heal reliably but can bleed substantially. Immobility after fracture drives systemic decompensation in frail patients.
additionalDifferentials: Pathological fracture from metastasis or myeloma
Osteoarthritis of the hip with acute-on-chronic pain
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs as first-line imaging
MRI (or CT) when a fracture is suspected clinically despite normal radiographs (occult fracture)
Full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, group and save/crossmatch as part of preoperative workup
ECG and assessment of cardiopulmonary fitness for anaesthesia
Bone mineral density assessment and metabolic bone screen for secondary fracture prevention
redFlags: Signs of significant blood loss or haemodynamic instability, particularly with subtrochanteric fractures
Pathological fracture features (bone destruction, minimal trauma in a younger patient) suggesting malignancy
Open fracture or associated neurovascular compromise of the limb
Prolonged surgical delay increasing mortality and complication risk in the frail elderly
reference.prognosis: Hip fracture in the elderly carries substantial morbidity and a significant one-year mortality driven by comorbidity; prompt surgery, early mobilisation, orthogeriatric care, and osteoporosis treatment improve functional recovery, though many patients do not regain full pre-injury independence.
pitfalls: Dismissing a hip fracture because the initial radiograph looks normal, missing an occult fracture
Delaying surgery unnecessarily for over-investigation of stable comorbidities
Choosing internal fixation for a displaced intracapsular fracture in an older patient, risking avascular necrosis and reoperation
Overlooking underlying osteoporosis and failing to institute secondary prevention
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Early surgery, generally within a day or two of admission, to reduce complications
Arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement) for displaced intracapsular fractures in older patients
Internal fixation to preserve the femoral head for undisplaced intracapsular fractures and in younger patients
Internal fixation with a dynamic hip screw or intramedullary device for extracapsular fractures
Multimodal analgesia including regional fascia iliaca nerve blocks, with venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
Orthogeriatric co-management with early mobilisation and prevention of delirium, pressure sores and chest infection
Osteoporosis treatment with bisphosphonates or other bone-protective agents plus falls prevention for secondary fracture prevention
